1619.title: First enslaved Africans brought to Jamestown
description: The first enslaved Africans were brought to Jamestown, Virginia, marking the beginning of slavery in what would become the United States.
This event laid the foundation for a system of forced labor that would persist for more than two centuries.

1641.title: Massachusetts Legalizes Slavery
description: Massachusetts becomes the first colony to legally recognize slavery through its Body of Liberties, setting a precedent for other colonies.

1662.title: Hereditary Slavery Law
description: Virginia enacts a law stating that children born to enslaved mothers inherit their status, establishing hereditary slavery in the colonies.

1705.title: Virginia Slave Codes
description: Virginia passes comprehensive slave codes defining the status of enslaved people and the rights of their owners, solidifying the institution of slavery.

1739.title: Stono Rebellion
description: The Stono Rebellion, one of the largest slave uprisings in the colonial period, takes place in South Carolina, leading to stricter slave laws.

1776.title: Declaration of Independence
description: The Declaration of Independence is adopted, asserting the principle of equality, though it does not address the issue of slavery, highlighting the contradictions in the nation's founding ideals.

1793.title: Fugitive Slave Act Passed
description: The Fugitive Slave Act of 1793 was enacted to provide for the return of enslaved people who escaped from one state into another state or territory. It allowed owners to capture and reclaim enslaved people who had fled to free states.
This law heightened tensions between North and South, as it required citizens and officials in free states to assist in the capture and return of escaped enslaved people.

1808.title: U.S. Bans the Transatlantic Slave Trade
description: The United States officially bans the importation of enslaved Africans, although illegal smuggling continues, marking a significant step in the abolitionist movement.

1830.title: Underground Railroad
description: From 1830 to 1865, the Underground Railroad was a network of secret routes and safe houses established in the United States during the early to mid-19th century. It was used by enslaved African Americans to escape into free states and Canada with the aid of abolitionists and allies who were sympathetic to their cause.
This covert system was instrumental in helping thousands of enslaved people gain their freedom and highlighted the widespread resistance to slavery in the United States.

1820.title: Missouri Compromise
description: The Missouri Compromise attempts to balance the number of slave and free states, illustrating the growing sectional conflict over slavery and the nation's struggle to maintain unity.

1831.title: Nat Turner's Rebellion
description: Nat Turner leads a significant slave rebellion in Virginia, resulting in stricter slave laws and increased tensions between North and South, highlighting the deep-seated resistance to slavery.

1850.title: Compromise of 1850 and Fugitive Slave Act
description: The Compromise of 1850 includes the Fugitive Slave Act, which mandates that escaped enslaved people be returned to their owners, even if found in free states, exacerbating sectional tensions.

1852.title: Publication of 'Uncle Tom's Cabin'
description: Harriet Beecher Stowe's novel 'Uncle Tom's Cabin' is published, galvanizing anti-slavery sentiment in the North and contributing to the abolitionist movement.

1857.title: Dred Scott Decision
description: The Supreme Court rules in Dred Scott v. Sandford that African Americans, whether free or enslaved, cannot be American citizens and have no standing to sue in federal court, deepening the national divide.

1860.title: Abraham Lincoln's Election
description: Abraham Lincoln is elected President of the United States on an anti-slavery platform, leading to the secession of Southern states and the onset of the Civil War.

intro.title: Emancipation / Reconstruction
intro.subtitle: Civil War, Chains Broken and a New Battle for Equality Begins.

1861.title: American Civil War
description: The Civil War was fought between the Northern states (the Union) and the Southern states (the Confederacy) primarily over the issue of slavery. Enslaved people played significant roles during the war, including working as laborers, serving as soldiers for the Union Army after the Emancipation Proclamation, and acting as spies and scouts.

The war resulted in the abolition of slavery but left the nation deeply divided, leading to a long and difficult period of Reconstruction aimed at integrating formerly enslaved people into American society and addressing the economic and social devastation of the South.

1862.title: Homestead Act
description: The Homestead Act is signed into law, providing land to settlers and encouraging Western migration, impacting freed slaves who sought new opportunities.

1863.title: Emancipation Proclamation
description: President Abraham Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation, declaring that all enslaved people in Confederate states were to be set free. This shifted the focus of the war towards the abolition of slavery and allowed African Americans to enlist in the Union Army.

The proclamation was a strategic move to weaken the Confederacy and gave the Union a moral cause. While it did not immediately free all enslaved people, it was a crucial step towards the eventual abolition of slavery and highlighted the Union's commitment to human rights.

1865.title: Lincoln Assassinated
description: President Abraham Lincoln is assassinated, creating uncertainty and upheaval during the early days of Reconstruction.

1866.title: Civil Rights Act of 1866
description: The Civil Rights Act of 1866 is passed, granting citizenship and equal protection under the law to African Americans.

1868.title: Fourteenth Amendment
description: The Fourteenth Amendment is ratified, ensuring citizenship and equal protection under the law for all persons born or naturalized in the United States.

1870.title: Fifteenth Amendment
description: The Fifteenth Amendment is ratified, granting African American men the right to vote and aiming to prevent racial discrimination in voting rights.

1871.title: Ku Klux Klan Act
description: Congress passes the Ku Klux Klan Act, authorizing federal action against the KKK and other white supremacist groups that terrorize African Americans.

1873.title: Colfax Massacre
description: The Colfax Massacre occurs in Louisiana, where white supremacists attack and kill dozens of African Americans defending a courthouse, illustrating the violent resistance to Reconstruction.

1877.title: Compromise of 1877
description: The Compromise of 1877 ends Reconstruction, withdrawing federal troops from the South and leading to the disenfranchisement and segregation of African Americans.

intro.title: Post-Reconstruction
intro.subtitle: Echoes of Freedom, Slavery Abolished but Discrimination Persists.

1878.title: Posse Comitatus Act
description: The Posse Comitatus Act of 1878 limited the use of federal troops in domestic law enforcement. This marked the end of federal intervention in the South.

1896.title: Plessy v. Ferguson
description: The Supreme Court's Plessy v. Ferguson decision in 1896 upheld the constitutionality of racial segregation. It established the doctrine of 'separate but equal.'

1909.title: Founding of the NAACP
description: The NAACP was founded in 1909 to fight for civil rights and combat racial discrimination. It became a leading organization in the civil rights movement.

1920.title: 19th Amendment Ratified
description: The 19th Amendment highlighted the intersection of gender and race in the fight for equality. Black women faced unique challenges, battling both sexism and racism.

1921.title: Tulsa Race Massacre
description: The Tulsa Race Massacre occurred in 1921, where a white mob attacked the prosperous Black neighborhood of Greenwood in Tulsa, Oklahoma. The massacre resulted in the deaths of hundreds of Black residents and the destruction of what was known as 'Black Wall Street.'

1948.title: Executive Order 9981
description: President Truman's Executive Order 9981 in 1948 desegregated the armed forces.This was a major step towards racial equality in the military.

1950.title: Sweatt v. Painter
description: The Supreme Court ruled in Sweatt v. Painter (1950) that separate but equal facilities are inherently unequal. This case challenged the doctrine of 'separate but equal.'

1954.title: Brown v. Board of Education
description: The Supreme Court decision in Brown v. Board of Education declared that racial segregation in public schools was unconstitutional. This landmark ruling overturned the 'separate but equal' doctrine.
The decision marked the beginning of the end for legal segregation in the United States and paved the way for further civil rights advancements.

1955.title: Montgomery Bus Boycott
description: Sparked by Rosa Parks' arrest, the Montgomery Bus Boycott became a pivotal event in the Civil Rights Movement. African Americans in Montgomery, Alabama, refused to ride city buses to protest segregated seating.
The boycott, led by Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., lasted for over a year and resulted in a Supreme Court ruling that segregation on public buses was unconstitutional.

1963.title: March on Washington
description: The March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom took place, where Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his famous 'I Have a Dream' speech. The march was one of the largest political rallies for human rights in U.S. history. It played a crucial role in building momentum for the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

1964.title: Civil Rights Act passed
description: The Civil Rights Act was passed, prohibiting discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. This landmark legislation addressed widespread racial discrimination and segregation.

1965.title: Voting Rights Act Passed
description: The Voting Rights Act was passed, eliminating various barriers to Black enfranchisement, such as literacy tests and other discriminatory practices. This act was significant in ensuring equal opportunity to vote.

1967.title: Loving v. Virginia decision
description: The Supreme Court decision in Loving v. Virginia struck down laws banning interracial marriage. This landmark case invalidated state laws prohibiting interracial marriage, ruling such laws violated the 14th Amendment.
The decision affirmed the right to marry regardless of race and helped dismantle remaining vestiges of legalized racial discrimination in the United States.

1968.title: Assassination of Martin Luther King Jr
description: On April 4, 1968, Martin Luther King Jr., leader of the Civil Rights Movement and advocate for nonviolent protest and racial equality, was assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee. His death marked a pivotal moment in American history, galvanizing the Civil Rights Movement, leading to the Fair Housing Act, and renewing efforts to address systemic racism and promote social justice.

1969.title: First Black Woman Elected to Congress
description: In 1969, Shirley Chisholm made history as the first African American woman elected to the United States Congress. Representing New York's 12th congressional district, she was a trailblazer.
Chisholm advocated for civil rights, women's rights, and social justice throughout her career, inspiring many and paving the way for future generations of women and minorities in politics.

1988.title: Civil Rights Restoration Act
description: The Civil Rights Restoration Act was passed, expanding non-discrimination laws to apply to entire institutions receiving federal funds, ensuring broader civil rights protections.
This legislative change promoted greater accountability and compliance.

2008.title: Barack Obama elected President
description: Barack Obama was elected as the first African American President of the United States, representing a historic milestone in American history and symbolizing progress in the struggle for racial equality.
Obama's presidency inspired many and highlighted the possibilities for achieving racial integration and representation in the highest office of the country, underscoring ongoing dialogues about race.

2010.title: Fair Sentencing Act
description: The Fair Sentencing Act of 2010 reduced the disparity between sentences for crack cocaine and powder cocaine offenses, which disproportionately affected Black Americans, promoting fairness.
By reducing the sentencing disparity, the Act aimed to address racial disparities in sentencing and ensure more equitable treatment under the law, marking a significant step towards justice.

2013.title: Black Lives Matter Movement
description: The Black Lives Matter (BLM) movement began in response to the acquittal of George Zimmerman in the shooting death of Trayvon Martin. BLM grew into an international activist movement.
The movement has played a crucial role in raising awareness about ongoing struggles faced by Black communities, advocating for significant changes in policies affecting racial justice.

2018.title: First Step Act
description: The First Step Act of 2018 is a bipartisan criminal justice reform law aimed at reducing recidivism and improving prison conditions, including provisions to reduce mandatory minimum sentences.
The Act seeks to improve rehabilitation programs and reentry initiatives for incarcerated individuals, addressing systemic issues in the criminal justice system affecting Black communities.

2020.title: George Floyd protests
description: The murder of George Floyd by a police officer in Minneapolis sparked nationwide and global protests against systemic racism and police brutality, calling for significant changes in policing.
This movement, marked by widespread demonstrations and public discourse on racism, highlighted enduring issues of racial inequality, leading to increased advocacy for civil rights.

2021.title: Juneteenth as a Federal Holiday
description: Juneteenth, commemorating the end of slavery, became a federal holiday in 2021, highlighting the importance of remembering and celebrating freedom and the ongoing fight for equality.

2024.title: Are we there yet?
description: If you had the patience to scroll all the way to here, then you might have a sense of just how early in the process we are for equal rights for the citizens descended from slavery in the USA. Despite significant strides in representation, legislation, and public awareness, systemic racism and inequality persist. The journey towards true equality continues, and each of us has a role to play in shaping a more just and inclusive society.
